pos: adv. (with effect; so as to produce the intended result)
etymology: From effectual, Latin efficere, to work out, accomplish, from ex- and facere, to do. An effect is a thing actually done; the adverb insists the working did not merely aim, it arrived.
biblical_def: Twice the Authorized Version says effectually, and both places are load-bearing walls of Reformed doctrine. The first is Paul on Peter: “For he that wrought effectually in Peter to the apostleship of the circumcision, the same was mighty in me toward the Gentiles” (Gal 2:8). Two apostles, two fields, one Worker — and the working is described not by what it attempted but by what it accomplished. The second is Paul on the Thessalonians' conversion: “ye received it not as the word of men, but as it is in truth, the word of God, which effectually worketh also in you that believe” (1Th 2:13). The word of God is not an offer lying inert until a man activates it; it is a working thing, and it works in those who believe. This is the whole difference between an effectual call and a general invitation. The gospel summons goes out broadly; the effectual call is that summons carried home by the Spirit so that the dead man rises. Paul says the same in Philippians without the adverb: “it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure” (Php 2:13) — the willing as well as the doing — and measures it by the power that raised Christ (Eph 1:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines effectually as with effect; efficaciously; in a manner to produce the intended effect; thoroughly; completely.
webster_full: EFFEC'TUALLY, adv.
With effect; efficaciously; in a manner to produce the intended effect.
The city was effectually defended.
Thoroughly; completely; as, the country was effectually subdued.
An effect is that which is produced; hence the adverb asserts not the attempt but the accomplishment.
scriptures: 1 Thessalonians 2:13

For this cause also thank we God without ceasing, because, when ye received the word of God which ye heard of us, ye received it not as the word of men, but as it is in truth, the word of God, which effectually worketh also in you that believe.
Galatians 2:8
(For he that wrought effectually in Peter to the apostleship of the circumcision, the same was mighty in me toward the Gentiles:)
Philippians 2:13
For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure.
Ephesians 1:19
And what is the exceeding greatness of his power to us-ward who believe, according to the working of his mighty power,
corruption_summary: The decisive adverb is quietly downgraded to a hopeful one, and God's working becomes God's offering.
corruption_paragraphs: Arminian and semi-Pelagian schemes must soften this word, because an effectual working leaves nothing for the creature's veto. So grace is re-described as enabling rather than accomplishing: God makes salvation possible, and the sinner makes it actual. 1 Thessalonians 2:13 does not read that way. The word of God is the subject and worketh is the verb, and Philippians 2:13 forecloses the last refuge by putting the willing itself inside God's working. If God works the will, the will is not the thing that finally decides.

The modern evangelistic method has absorbed the error at the level of technique rather than doctrine. The appeal is engineered, the music is timed, the decision is counted, and the result is measured in hands raised — because if the call is not effectual in itself, something must be added to make it land. Reformed practice preaches the word plainly and expects it to work, since the working was never the preacher's to supply. Galatians 2:8 gives the pattern: the same One wrought in Peter and in Paul, in fields as different as Jerusalem and Ephesus, and the difference in the harvest was never a difference in the men.
roots_summary: Greek energeo (G1754), to work, to be operative; energes (G1756), active, effectual; Latin efficere, to accomplish.
roots_lines: Greek energeitai (G1754) — is at work, is operative; the verb in 1 Thessalonians 2:13, active and continuous.
Greek energesas (G1754) — having worked effectively; Galatians 2:8 of the One who wrought in Peter.
Greek energeia (G1753) — operative power; Ephesians 1:19, measured by the raising of Christ.
Greek eudokia (G2107) — good pleasure; Philippians 2:13, the ground of the working is God's own delight.
Latin efficere, from ex- and facere — to work out to completion; Webster's root.
usage: “Which effectually worketh also in you that believe” — the word is a worker, not a proposal.
“He that wrought effectually in Peter” — one Worker, two apostles, two fields.
“Both to will and to do” — the willing is inside the working, not prior to it.

pos: n. (the state of being new; novelty; freshness of life or spirit)
etymology: From new, Saxon niwe, with the noun-ending -ness. Twice in the Authorized Version, both in Romans, and both describing the manner of a Christian's living rather than the date of his conversion.
biblical_def: Both occurrences belong to Paul and both stand at the hinge of the Christian life. The first is the fruit of union with Christ in His death and resurrection: “Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life” (Rom 6:4). Note the logic. The newness is not an improvement bolted onto the old man; it is the walking that follows a burial. The old man was crucified with Him (Rom 6:6), and what walks out is new. The second occurrence contrasts two ways of serving God: “that we should serve in newness of spirit, and not in the oldness of the letter” (Rom 7:6). The Christian is not a Pharisee with better manners; he serves from a changed nature, not from an external code held over a dead heart. Paul states the same doctrine as a verdict in 2 Corinthians: “Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new” (2Co 5:17). Newness in Scripture is therefore always derived — it comes out of a grave, and it is Christ's resurrection life expressing itself in a man's ordinary Tuesday.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines newness as lateness of origin; recentness; novelty; innovation; and also a different state or qualities introduced by change or regeneration.
webster_full: NEW'NESS, n.
1. Lateness of origin; recentness; state of being lately invented or produced; as the newness of a dress.
2. Novelty; the state of being first known or introduced.
3. Innovation; recent change.
4. Want of practice or familiarity. 5. Different state or qualities introduced by change or regeneration. That we should walk in newness of life. Rom. 6.
scriptures: Romans 6:4
Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life.
Romans 7:6
But now we are delivered from the law, that being dead wherein we were held; that we should serve in newness of spirit, and not in the oldness of the letter.
Romans 6:6
Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin.
2 Corinthians 5:17
Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.
corruption_summary: Newness is preached as a fresh start the sinner makes rather than a resurrection life he is given.
corruption_paragraphs: The revivalist tradition has long offered newness as a turning over of a new leaf — a decision, a rededication, a clean page in January. Romans 6:4 puts a funeral between the old and the new. There is no new walking that does not come out of a burial with Christ, and a man who has not died with Him has not begun. This is why Reformed teaching insists regeneration precedes faith: the newness is not the reward of the sinner's effort but the cause of his believing.

The therapeutic version is subtler. It reads 2 Corinthians 5:17 as a promise about self-perception — you are a new creature, so think better of yourself — when Paul is making an objective statement about a man's standing and nature in Christ, not a suggestion about his self-image. And Romans 7:6 blocks the opposite ditch, where newness becomes an excuse to despise the law altogether. The Christian is delivered from the law as a covenant of works; he is not delivered into lawlessness. He serves — that verb stays — but in newness of spirit.
roots_summary: Greek kainotes (G2538), newness of kind; kainos (G2537), new in quality as opposed to neos, new in time.
roots_lines: Greek kainotes (G2538) — newness; both Romans 6:4 and 7:6 use this noun and no other place does.
Greek kainos (G2537) — new in kind, fresh in nature; distinguished from neos (G3501), new merely in time.
Greek palaiotes (G3821) — oldness; the deliberate opposite in Romans 7:6, the letter grown stale.
Greek kaine ktisis (G2537, G2937) — new creature, new creation; 2 Corinthians 5:17.
Saxon niwe — new; Webster's root, and the -ness that makes the adjective a state.
usage: “Walk in newness of life” — walking, which is daily, out of a burial, which was once.
“Newness of spirit, and not in the oldness of the letter” — the service continues; the power changes.
“He is a new creature” — a statement of fact, not a suggestion about self-image.

pos: n. (firmness of standing; fixedness in place, principle, or faith)
etymology: Saxon stede, a place or station, and fast, firm — literally fixed in place. The Authorized Version keeps the older single-d spelling throughout; modern printings usually read steadfastness.
biblical_def: The word means fixed where you were set, and Scripture uses it twice, once as a commendation and once as a warning. Paul, writing to a church he had never visited, says he is “joying and beholding your order, and the stedfastness of your faith in Christ” (Col 2:5) — order and stedfastness together, the two things a church under pressure from philosophy and false humility most needed. Peter uses the same noun to say it can be lost: “beware lest ye also, being led away with the error of the wicked, fall from your own stedfastness” (2Pe 3:17). The falling is not from salvation but from a footing; a believer led away by error loses his standing-ground and must be recovered. That is why the apostolic commands attach stedfastness to work rather than to feeling: “be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1Co 15:58). And Hebrews ties it to the end rather than the beginning: “we are made partakers of Christ, if we hold the beginning of our confidence stedfast unto the end” (Heb 3:14). Perseverance and stedfastness are the same doctrine seen from two sides — God keeps His own, and His own hold fast; the second is the evidence of the first.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines stedfastness as firmness of standing; fixedness in place; firm adherence to opinion or principle; constancy; resolution.
webster_full: STED'FASTNESS, n. [from stedfast.]
1. Fixedness in place; firmness of standing.
2. Firm adherence to opinion or principle; constancy; resolution; steadiness.
Beware lest ye fall from your own stedfastness. 2 Pet. 3.
The word is compounded of stede, a place or station, and fast, firm; that is, firm in its place.
scriptures: Colossians 2:5
For though I be absent in the flesh, yet am I with you in the spirit, joying and beholding your order, and the stedfastness of your faith in Christ.
2 Peter 3:17
Ye therefore, beloved, seeing ye know these things before, beware lest ye also, being led away with the error of the wicked, fall from your own stedfastness.
1 Corinthians 15:58
Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
Hebrews 3:14
For we are made partakers of Christ, if we hold the beginning of our confidence stedfast unto the end;
corruption_summary: Fixedness is now called rigidity, and the man who will not move is treated as the problem rather than the anchor.
corruption_paragraphs: The age has reversed the valuation. To be fixed in principle is to be closed; to be moveable is to be humble and growing. So the doctrinal statement is loosened every decade, the confession becomes a historical document rather than a boundary, and the minister who holds the old line is described as unable to engage. Colossians 2:5 places order and stedfastness among the things an apostle rejoices to see. They are not a failure of imagination. They are what a church looks like when the philosophy of the age has been offered and refused.

2 Peter 3:17 supplies the reason the pressure is applied at all. Men are led away; the falling is not a slow drift but a following. That is why the Reformed churches bind themselves to a subordinate standard — not to freeze thought, but because a congregation that has fixed in writing what it believes can tell when it is being moved. Stedfastness is not the refusal to learn. It is the refusal to be led away, which is a different thing entirely, and 1 Corinthians 15:58 shows it is measured in labour, not in stubbornness.
roots_summary: Greek stereoma (G4733), a solid frame, firmness; bebaios (G949), firm, sure; sterigmos (G4740), stability.
roots_lines: Greek stereoma (G4733) — a solid structure, firmament, battle-line; Colossians 2:5, the stedfastness of their faith.
Greek sterigmos (G4740) — a fixed position, stability; 2 Peter 3:17, the footing a man may fall from.
Greek hedraios (G1476) — seated, settled; 1 Corinthians 15:58, rendered stedfast alongside ametakinetos, unmoveable.
Greek bebaian…mechri telous (G949) — firm unto the end; Hebrews 3:14, where the holding proves the partaking.
Saxon stede and fast — place and firm; Webster's root, the picture of a man who stays where he was stationed.
usage: “Your order, and the stedfastness of your faith” — an apostle rejoicing over both.
“Fall from your own stedfastness” — a footing is lost by being led, not by drifting.
“Stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding” — measured in labour, not in obstinacy.

pos: n. (a receiving with approbation; the state of being accepted or acceptable)
etymology: From accept, Latin acceptare, to take willingly, from ad- and capere, to take. The single Authorized Version occurrence is sacrificial — it is about what comes up on an altar.
biblical_def: The noun occurs once, in Isaiah's vision of the nations streaming to Zion: “All the flocks of Kedar shall be gathered together unto thee, the rams of Nebaioth shall minister unto thee: they shall come up with acceptance on mine altar, and I will glorify the house of my glory” (Isa 60:7). Acceptance in Scripture is therefore first an altar word. It is not a mood in God and not a self-assessment in man; it is the verdict pronounced over a sacrifice that God Himself has appointed. The New Testament carries the same freight and names the ground: “To the praise of the glory of his grace, wherein he hath made us accepted in the beloved” (Eph 1:6). The believer is not accepted on his own footing at all; he is accepted in Another, and the Beloved is the reason the altar receives him. From that settled standing flows the believer's daily offering — “present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service” (Rom 12:1) — and his ambition: “we labour, that, whether present or absent, we may be accepted of him” (2Co 5:9). Note the order. Acceptance of the person comes first and is complete in Christ; acceptableness of the works follows and is the fruit.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines acceptance as a receiving with approbation or satisfaction; favorable reception; and the state of being acceptable.
webster_full: ACCEPT'ANCE, n.
1. A receiving with approbation or satisfaction; favorable reception.
They shall come up with acceptance on my altar. Isa. 60.
2. The receiving of a bill of exchange or order, in such a manner as to bind the acceptor to make payment.
3. The state of being acceptable; as, a man in good acceptance with his superiors.
scriptures: Isaiah 60:7

All the flocks of Kedar shall be gathered together unto thee, the rams of Nebaioth shall minister unto thee: they shall come up with acceptance on mine altar, and I will glorify the house of my glory.
Ephesians 1:6
To the praise of the glory of his grace, wherein he hath made us accepted in the beloved.
Romans 12:1
I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service.
2 Corinthians 5:9
Wherefore we labour, that, whether present or absent, we may be accepted of him.
corruption_summary: Acceptance has been detached from the altar and re-founded on the self, so that God is said to accept a man as he is rather than in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The governing slogan of the age is that God accepts you as you are, and it is half a truth doing the work of a whole lie. God does receive sinners as they are, in the sense that no man cleans himself up first. But Ephesians 1:6 says where the receiving happens: in the beloved. Acceptance is mediated. Strike out the Mediator and the sentence becomes a statement about divine indifference to sin, which is precisely how affirming theology now uses it — to bless what Scripture names as sin on the ground that the sinner is accepted. Isaiah's picture is the rebuke: the rams of Nebaioth come up on mine altar, and it is the altar that makes the coming acceptable.

The therapeutic corruption runs alongside. Acceptance becomes self-acceptance, a psychological task in which a man makes peace with himself, and the gospel is recruited as its endorsement. Scripture never asks a man to accept himself; it tells him he is accepted in Another, which is a far stronger comfort because it does not depend on his opinion of himself on any given morning. And it is stronger still because it is not the end of the matter: Romans 12:1 turns the accepted man out of doors with his body on the altar. Standing is settled; service has only begun.
roots_summary: Hebrew ratson (H7522), good pleasure, acceptance, favour; Greek charitoo (G5487), to bestow grace upon; Latin acceptare, to take willingly.
roots_lines: Hebrew ratson (H7522) — delight, favour, acceptance; the altar word of Isaiah 60:7 and of Leviticus 1:3.
Greek echaritosen (G5487) — He has graced us, made us objects of grace; Ephesians 1:6, in the beloved.
Greek euarestos (G2101) — well-pleasing, acceptable; Romans 12:1 of the living sacrifice.
Greek euarestoi einai auto (G2101) — to be well-pleasing to Him; 2 Corinthians 5:9, the labour of the already-accepted.
Latin acceptare, from ad- and capere — to take to oneself willingly; Webster's root.
usage: “They shall come up with acceptance on mine altar” — the altar makes the coming acceptable.
“Accepted in the beloved” — the preposition is the whole doctrine.
“Holy, acceptable unto God” — the works follow the standing; they do not buy it.

pos: n. (the doing or carrying out of a thing; the completion of what was promised or begun)
etymology: From perform, Old French parfournir, to furnish or accomplish completely, from par- (thoroughly) and fournir, to furnish. The old sense is carrying through to completion, not a display before an audience.
biblical_def: Both occurrences concern promises being carried through. Elisabeth says to Mary, “blessed is she that believed: for there shall be a performance of those things which were told her from the Lord” (Luk 1:45). The beatitude is pronounced on faith, and the ground of it is that God finishes what He announces — Mary is blessed not because she achieved anything but because she believed a promise that would certainly be performed. Paul uses the word of a very ordinary matter, the Corinthian collection for the poor saints: “Now therefore perform the doing of it; that as there was a readiness to will, so there may be a performance also out of that which ye have” (2Co 8:11). Willing is not the same as doing; a readiness that never becomes a gift is unfinished, and Paul asks for the completion. Put together, the two texts hold the whole Reformed doctrine of the Christian life: God performs His promises infallibly — “he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Php 1:6) — and believers are therefore commanded to perform their duties really. Abraham is the pattern of the first: “being fully persuaded that, what he had promised, he was able also to perform” (Rom 4:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines performance as the act of performing; execution or completion of any thing; the carrying into effect a promise, purpose, or covenant.
webster_full: PERFORM'ANCE, n.
1. Execution or completion of any thing; a doing; as the performance of work or of an undertaking.
2. The fulfilment of a promise or covenant; as the performance of a vow.
3. Action; deed; thing done; as a virtuous performance.
4. Composition; work written. The old sense is to carry through to completion, from par, thoroughly, and fournir, to furnish.
scriptures: Luke 1:45
And blessed is she that believed: for there shall be a performance of those things which were told her from the Lord.
2 Corinthians 8:11
Now therefore perform the doing of it; that as there was a readiness to will, so there may be a performance also out of that which ye have.
Philippians 1:6
Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ:
Romans 4:21
And being fully persuaded that, what he had promised, he was able also to perform.
corruption_summary: The word has slid from completing a promise to putting on a show, and the church has caught the disease in both directions.
corruption_paragraphs: English moved performance from the covenant to the stage, and the church followed. A worship service is now assessed the way a concert is: the music performed, the sermon delivered, the room responding. Luke 1:45 uses the word for something no audience watches — a promise being carried through over nine months in an unmarried girl in Nazareth. The regulative principle exists in part to keep this distinction: what is done in the assembly is done because God commanded it, which means no one on the platform is performing and no one in the pews is an audience.

The opposite corruption is a lazy reading of Philippians 1:6. Because God performs the good work, it is said, the believer's own performing does not much matter — and effort is treated as a hint of legalism. 2 Corinthians 8:11 is unembarrassed: Paul tells a willing church to go and actually do it. The Reformed order is God works, therefore you work (Php 2:12-13), never God works, therefore you need not. A readiness to will that never yields a performance is not humility about grace; it is an unfinished obedience.
roots_summary: Greek teleiosis (G5050), a completing, fulfilment; epiteleo (G2005), to finish, accomplish; Old French parfournir, to furnish completely.
roots_lines: Greek teleiosis (G5050) — completion, fulfilment; Luke 1:45, there shall be a finishing of what was told her.
Greek epitelesate (G2005) — complete it, bring it to its end; 2 Corinthians 8:11, the command to the willing.
Greek epitelesei (G2005) — He will complete it; Philippians 1:6, the same verb with God as subject.
Greek dunatos…poiesai (G1415) — able also to do; Romans 4:21, Abraham's persuasion about God's power to perform.
Old French parfournir — to furnish thoroughly; Webster's root, with completion and not display in view.
usage: “There shall be a performance of those things” — the beatitude rests on God finishing, not on Mary achieving.
“A readiness to will, so there may be a performance” — willing is not yet doing.
“Will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ” — the same verb, with God as the subject.

pos: n. (readiness; eagerness; promptness of mind to act)
etymology: From forward, Saxon foreweard, toward the front. In the Authorized Version the sense is the good one — eagerness, readiness of mind — not the modern pejorative of boldness or impertinence.
biblical_def: Both occurrences belong to Paul's two chapters on the collection for the poor saints at Jerusalem, and both mean a readiness of mind that runs ahead of being told. “I speak not by commandment, but by occasion of the forwardness of others, and to prove the sincerity of your love” (2Co 8:8). Paul deliberately refuses to issue an order; he sets the eagerness of the Macedonians in front of the Corinthians and lets it do the work, because a gift extracted by command proves nothing about love. And again: “For I know the forwardness of your mind, for which I boast of you to them of Macedonia, that Achaia was ready a year ago; and your zeal hath provoked very many” (2Co 9:2). Forwardness is contagious, and Paul is candid about using it that way. But he guards it from becoming a measure of the purse: “if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not” (2Co 8:12). The willing mind is the thing weighed. Paul owns the same eagerness himself in the same cause — “they would that we should remember the poor; the same which I also was forward to do” (Gal 2:10) — and it is a word the modern English has soured without cause.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines forwardness as readiness; promptness; eagerness; ardor; and also, in a less favorable sense, assurance or want of due reserve.
webster_full: FOR'WARDNESS, n.
1. Cheerful readiness; promptness; as the forwardness of Christians in propagating the gospel.
It expresses more than willingness.
2. Eagerness; ardor; as the forwardness of a young man.
3. Boldness; confidence; assurance; want of due reserve or modesty. In this sense the word is used reproachfully.
scriptures: 2 Corinthians 8:8
I speak not by commandment, but by occasion of the forwardness of others, and to prove the sincerity of your love.
2 Corinthians 9:2
For I know the forwardness of your mind, for which I boast of you to them of Macedonia, that Achaia was ready a year ago; and your zeal hath provoked very many.
2 Corinthians 8:12
For if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not.
Galatians 2:10
Only they would that we should remember the poor; the same which I also was forward to do.
corruption_summary: Giving is now moved by pressure, quota, and appeal-craft, exactly the machinery Paul refused to use.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Corinthians 8:8 is the plainest apostolic statement on fundraising in the New Testament, and it is almost universally ignored. Paul will not command. He declines the one instrument every modern appeal reaches for first — obligation — because the point of the collection is to prove the sincerity of your love, and a proof obtained under compulsion proves nothing. The tithe-as-law preaching, the pledge card, the thermometer on the wall, the guilt-shaped appeal letter: all of them get money and none of them get what Paul was after.

The prosperity variant is worse, because it converts forwardness into an investment. Give eagerly and God will return it multiplied — so the eagerness is self-interested and the poor saints at Jerusalem become a vehicle. Paul's guard is 2 Corinthians 8:12: the willing mind is accepted according to what a man hath, not what he has not. That single clause frees the poor widow from shame and strips the wealthy donor of leverage. Giving in Scripture is measured by readiness of mind, and God loves a cheerful giver (2Co 9:7) because cheerfulness is what commandment cannot manufacture.
roots_summary: Greek spoude (G4710), haste, earnestness, diligence; prothumia (G4288), readiness of mind; Saxon foreweard, toward the front.
roots_lines: Greek spoude (G4710) — earnest haste, diligence; 2 Corinthians 8:8, the forwardness of the Macedonians.
Greek prothumia (G4288) — forwardness of mind, eager willingness; 2 Corinthians 9:2, and the same root in Romans 1:15.
Greek prothumos (G4289) — ready, willing; the spirit is willing in Matthew 26:41.
Greek euprosdektos (G2144) — well-accepted; 2 Corinthians 8:12, the willing mind is what is received.
Saxon foreweard — toward the front; Webster's root, before the English soured to impertinence.
usage: “I speak not by commandment” — the one lever every modern appeal pulls first, and Paul refused it.
“Your zeal hath provoked very many” — eagerness is contagious, and Paul says so plainly.
“Accepted according to that a man hath” — the widow is freed and the donor is disarmed.

etymology: Latin liberalitas, from liberalis, befitting a free man, from liber, free. In the Authorized Version it means open-handed generosity — the older English sense, entirely distinct from the political and theological uses the word has since acquired.
biblical_def: The word means bounty in giving, and the Authorized Version uses it twice, both of the same relief fund for the poor saints at Jerusalem. “And when I come, whomsoever ye shall approve by your letters, them will I send to bring your liberality unto Jerusalem” (1Co 16:3) — note the care about handling other men's money, with approved messengers and written credentials. The second occurrence contains the whole Christian doctrine of generosity in one sentence: “How that in a great trial of affliction the abundance of their joy and their deep poverty abounded unto the riches of their liberality” (2Co 8:2). Every term in it cuts against expectation. The givers were in a great trial of affliction, not prosperity; their poverty is called deep; and out of that came riches of liberality. The arithmetic is impossible and Paul knows it. Its explanation comes a few verses later, and it is Christological rather than financial: “ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich” (2Co 8:9). Christian liberality is the imitation of an impoverishment. That is also why it must be free: “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2Co 9:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines liberality as munificence; bounty; that disposition of heart which inclines men to give largely; and largeness of mind free from narrow views.
webster_full: LIBERAL'ITY, n. [L. liberalitas.]
1. Munificence; bounty. That disposition of heart which inclines men to part with their property for the relief of others.
2. A particular act of generosity; a gift; a gratuity. Sometimes it may be synonymous with charity, but it has a more general signification.
3. Largeness of mind; catholicism; that comprehensiveness of mind which includes other interests beside its own.
The word is from liber, free; the liberality of Scripture is the bounty of a free man, not a political disposition.
scriptures: 2 Corinthians 8:2
How that in a great trial of affliction the abundance of their joy and their deep poverty abounded unto the riches of their liberality.
1 Corinthians 16:3
And when I come, whomsoever ye shall approve by your letters, them will I send to bring your liberality unto Jerusalem.
2 Corinthians 8:9
For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich.
2 Corinthians 9:7
Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.
corruption_summary: The word has been captured by politics, so that liberality now names a party rather than a bounty, and generosity is outsourced to the state.
corruption_paragraphs: The English word has been so thoroughly annexed by political vocabulary that its biblical sense is nearly unreadable. Worse, the annexation has carried a doctrine with it: that generosity is achieved by policy, and a man discharges his obligation to the poor by voting. 2 Corinthians 8:2 describes something no legislature can produce — churches in deep poverty and great affliction giving out of joy. Transfer is not liberality; liberality is a disposition of the heart of a free man toward a neighbour he could have ignored. The Macedonian gift cost the givers, and that is why Paul writes a whole chapter about it.

Inside the church the corruption runs the other way — into machinery. 1 Corinthians 16:3 shows the apostolic care: approved men, letters, transparency about other people's money, because liberality that is not handled honestly stops being liberality and becomes an occasion for scandal. And 2 Corinthians 9:7 forbids the two engines most commonly used to raise it: grudging and necessity. Whatever is squeezed out of a congregation by obligation may be money, but it is not the thing Scripture calls by this name.
roots_summary: Greek haplotes (G572), singleness, simplicity, liberality; charis (G5485), grace, gift; Latin liberalitas, from liber, free.
roots_lines: Greek haplotes (G572) — singleness of heart, and so open-handedness; 2 Corinthians 8:2, a generosity with no double motive in it.
Greek charis (G5485) — grace, and by extension a gracious gift; 1 Corinthians 16:3, the liberality is literally your grace.
Greek hilaron doten (G2431) — a cheerful giver; 2 Corinthians 9:7, the root of English hilarious.
Greek eptocheusen (G4433) — He became poor, beggared Himself; 2 Corinthians 8:9, the pattern being imitated.
Latin liber, free — Webster's root; liberality is the bounty proper to a free man.
usage: “Their deep poverty abounded unto the riches of their liberality” — arithmetic that only grace explains.
“Whomsoever ye shall approve by your letters” — other men's money, handled in the open.
“Though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor” — the pattern and the power.

pos: adv. (to a sufficient degree; enough; adequately)
etymology: From sufficient, Latin sufficere, to be enough, from sub- and facere, to make under or supply. The idea is supply that meets the need exactly — neither short nor superfluous.
biblical_def: The adverb appears twice, and the two uses face opposite directions. The first is an honest confession of shortfall in Hezekiah's passover: “For they could not keep it at that time, because the priests had not sanctified themselves sufficiently, neither had the people gathered themselves together to Jerusalem” (2Ch 30:3). The feast had to be moved a month because the ministers were not ready — a remarkable admission for Scripture to record about the clergy, and a standing rebuke to any notion that the ordinances may be handled carelessly. The second is a promise of enough: Tyre's merchandise shall at last be holiness to the LORD, “for them that dwell before the LORD, to eat sufficiently, and for durable clothing” (Isa 23:18). The servants of God are promised food enough and clothing that lasts — not abundance for hoarding, since the same verse says it shall not be treasured nor laid up. Behind both stands the great New Testament use of the root, which places all sufficiency outside the man: “Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think any thing as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is of God” (2Co 3:5); and the Lord's own word to Paul, “My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness” (2Co 12:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sufficiently as to a sufficient degree; enough; to a degree that answers the purpose or gives content.
webster_full: SUFFI'CIENTLY, adv.
To a sufficient degree; enough; to a degree that answers the purpose, or gives content; as, we are sufficiently supplied with food.
A man sufficiently qualified for the office.
The Latin sufficere is to be enough, to suffice; the idea is a supply adequate to the need.
The priests had not sanctified themselves sufficiently. 2 Chron. 30.
scriptures: 2 Chronicles 30:3
For they could not keep it at that time, because the priests had not sanctified themselves sufficiently, neither had the people gathered themselves together to Jerusalem.
Isaiah 23:18

And her merchandise and her hire shall be holiness to the LORD: it shall not be treasured nor laid up; for her merchandise shall be for them that dwell before the LORD, to eat sufficiently, and for durable clothing.
2 Corinthians 3:5
Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think any thing as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is of God;
2 Corinthians 12:9

And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
corruption_summary: Self-sufficiency is preached as a virtue and enough is treated as a failure, so the one thing Scripture calls sufficient is the one thing men will not accept.
corruption_paragraphs: The culture's highest compliment is self-sufficiency, and 2 Corinthians 3:5 denies a man even the capacity to think anything as of himself. That is a total claim, and it is the death of the self-made ministry as much as of the self-made man. The corruption enters the church whenever competence is treated as the qualification and the sufficiency is located in gifting, training, or platform. Paul was the ablest man in the first century and disclaimed sufficiency for a thought.

The other corruption is dissatisfaction with enough. Isaiah 23:18 promises food sufficient and clothing durable, and explicitly rules out treasuring and laying up — which most readers experience as a disappointment rather than a promise. And 2 Corinthians 12:9 is routinely quoted as a consolation prize for people whose prayers were declined, when it is in fact the answer: the grace is the sufficiency, and the weakness is where the strength is perfected. A church that cannot preach enough as a blessing will always be vulnerable to a gospel of more.
roots_summary: Hebrew lemadai, to sufficiency; Greek hikanos (G2425), sufficient, competent; arkeo (G714), to be enough; Latin sufficere.
roots_lines: Hebrew lemikhsah and lesobe'ah — for covering and for satisfying; Isaiah 23:18, food to the full and clothing that lasts.
Greek hikanoi (G2425) — sufficient, competent, adequate; 2 Corinthians 3:5, denied to the self and granted from God.
Greek hikanotes (G2426) — sufficiency; the noun in the same verse, our sufficiency is of God.
Greek arkei (G714) — it is enough, it suffices; 2 Corinthians 12:9, my grace is sufficient for thee.
Latin sufficere, from sub- and facere — to supply underneath; Webster's root, a supply that meets the need.
usage: “The priests had not sanctified themselves sufficiently” — the feast waited a month for unready ministers.
“To eat sufficiently, and for durable clothing” — enough, and not laid up.
“Our sufficiency is of God” — not even a thought is self-supplied.

pos: adv. (with sound mind; temperately; without excess or extravagance of thought or appetite)
etymology: From sober, Latin sobrius, from se- (without) and ebrius (drunk). The literal sense is unintoxicated, and Scripture extends it from the cup to the mind — a man may be drunk on his own estimate of himself.
biblical_def: The Authorized Version uses soberly twice, and neither one is about wine. The first governs a man's estimate of himself: “not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think soberly, according as God hath dealt to every man the measure of faith” (Rom 12:3). Sobriety of mind is the opposite of intoxication with oneself, and Paul gives it a fixed standard — the measure of faith God has dealt. That standard cuts both ways: a man may be drunk on his own importance, and he may equally be drunk on his own worthlessness, since both are estimates formed without reference to what God has actually given. The second occurrence makes it a whole way of life: grace is “teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world” (Tit 2:12) — soberly toward self, righteously toward neighbour, godly toward God. The related commands add urgency: “Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour” (1Pe 5:8), and “let us not sleep, as do others; but let us watch and be sober” (1Th 5:6). Sobriety is a soldier's clarity, not a temperament.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines soberly as without intemperance; without excess; moderately; temperately; and with sound reason, calmly and coolly.
webster_full: SO'BERLY, adv.
1. Without intemperance or excess; as, to live soberly.
2. Without enthusiasm or extravagance; coolly; calmly; moderately.
3. Gravely; seriously; with sound reason.
4. Without heat or passion. Let us think soberly of ourselves, according to the measure of faith. Rom. 12.
scriptures: Romans 12:3

For I say, through the grace given unto me, to every man that is among you, not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think soberly, according as God hath dealt to every man the measure of faith.
Titus 2:12
Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world;
1 Peter 5:8
Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour:
1 Thessalonians 5:6
Therefore let us not sleep, as do others; but let us watch and be sober.
corruption_summary: Self-esteem teaching and its mirror image both violate Romans 12:3, because both estimate the self without reference to what God has dealt.
corruption_paragraphs: A generation of church teaching baptized the self-esteem movement, discovering in Scripture a mandate to think better of oneself, usually by way of a mangled reading of love thy neighbour as thyself. Romans 12:3 forbids thinking more highly than one ought and supplies the ruler: according as God hath dealt to every man the measure of faith. That is an external standard. It makes sober thought possible precisely because it is not self-generated — a man does not have to talk himself up or talk himself down; he has to look at what God gave.

The reaction against that error can become its twin. A self-loathing that dwells on its own wretchedness is still a man drunk on himself, only bitterly, and it is no more sober than the other. It also tends to excuse: the man who declares himself worthless has quietly relieved himself of the duty attached to the measure he was dealt. Titus 2:12 keeps the whole thing from turning inward at all, because grace teaches soberly, righteously, and godly — self, neighbour, and God in one movement. And 1 Peter 5:8 gives the reason clarity matters: a lion is in the field, and drunk men are what lions eat.
roots_summary: Greek sophroneo (G4993), to be of sound mind; sophronos (G4996), soberly, sensibly; nepho (G3525), to be sober, watchful; Latin sobrius.
roots_lines: Greek sophronein (G4993) — to be of sound mind, to think sanely; Romans 12:3, set against huperphronein, to over-think oneself.
Greek sophronos (G4996) — soberly, with self-control; Titus 2:12, first of the three adverbs grace teaches.
Greek nepsate (G3525) — be sober, unintoxicated, clear-headed; 1 Peter 5:8, paired with vigilance.
Greek metron pisteos (G3358, G4102) — the measure of faith; the external ruler that makes sober thought possible.
Latin sobrius, from se- and ebrius — not drunk; Webster's root, carried from the cup to the mind.
usage: “Not to think of himself more highly than he ought” — and the ruler is what God dealt, not what he feels.
“Soberly, righteously, and godly” — toward self, neighbour, and God, in one breath.
“Be sober, be vigilant” — because there is a lion in the field.

pos: n. (elevation; loftiness; and in the Authorized Version, the exalted majesty of God)
etymology: From high, Saxon heah, with the noun-ending -ness. In English it became a title of address for princes; in the Authorized Version it belongs to God, and it is a terror before it is an honour.
biblical_def: The word occurs twice and in both places it is God's, not a prince's. Job names it as the thing that kept him from injustice: “For destruction from God was a terror to me, and by reason of his highness I could not endure” (Job 31:23). This is the close of Job's great oath of innocence, where he lists what he never did to the poor, the widow, the fatherless, and the hired man — and his reason is not policy or reputation but that he could not stand upright under the thought of God's exaltedness. The fear of God is here a working restraint on a powerful man's treatment of weak people, which is exactly what a doctrine of divine transcendence is for. The second occurrence stands in Isaiah's oracle against Babylon: “I have commanded my sanctified ones, I have also called my mighty ones for mine anger, even them that rejoice in my highness” (Isa 13:3). The same highness that terrified Job is rejoiced in by those He summons. Both responses are right, and together they are the whole creaturely posture before the God who sits “upon a throne, high and lifted up” (Isa 6:1), of whom the psalmist asks, “Who is like unto the LORD our God, who dwelleth on high” (Psa 113:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines highness as elevation above the surface; loftiness; dignity; and a title of honor given to princes — though in Scripture it is used of the excellency of God.
webster_full: HIGH'NESS, n.
1. Elevation above the surface; loftiness; altitude; height.
2. Dignity; elevation in rank, character or power.
3. Excellence; value.
4. Violence; as the highness of wind. 5. Great degree; as the highness of a crime. 6. A title of honor given to princes. By reason of his highness I could not endure. Job 31.
scriptures: For destruction from God was a terror to me, and by reason of his highness I could not endure.
Isaiah 13:3
I have commanded my sanctified ones, I have also called my mighty ones for mine anger, even them that rejoice in my highness.
Isaiah 6:1
In the year that king Uzziah died I saw also the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and his train filled the temple.
Psalm 113:5
Who is like unto the LORD our God, who dwelleth on high,
corruption_summary: Divine highness has been traded for divine relatability, and with it went the only thing that reliably restrains men who have power over others.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern religion prefers a God who is near and dislikes a God who is high, and the preference has been dressed up as a recovery of intimacy. Job 31:23 shows what is lost in the exchange. A wealthy and powerful man lists everything he might have done to his servants, to widows, to the fatherless — and says he did not do it because he could not endure under God's highness. Transcendence was the brake. Where God is merely a friend, that brake is released, and the history of abusive ministry in the last half-century is largely the history of men who preached a very approachable God to people they were mistreating.

Open theism and process theology attack the same attribute at the doctrinal level, lowering God into time, contingency, and mutability so that He may be more genuinely responsive. What they produce is a God who cannot be the refuge Psalm 113:5 offers, because a God who dwells on high is the only one with a floor firm enough to stand on. Isaiah 13:3 gives the answer to the charge that highness makes God cold: His own sanctified ones are described as those who rejoice in it. The elevation that terrifies the guilty is the delight of the redeemed.
roots_summary: Hebrew se'eth (H7613), exaltation, dignity, rising; ga'avah (H1346), majesty, highness; Saxon heah, high.
roots_lines: Hebrew se'eth (H7613) — a lifting up, exaltation, dignity; Job 31:23, the highness under which Job could not endure.
Hebrew ga'avah (H1346) — majesty, excellency; Isaiah 13:3, and the same root that in men becomes pride.
Hebrew ram venissa (H7311, H5375) — high and lifted up; Isaiah 6:1, the throne vision Job's word anticipates.
Hebrew hammagbihi lashabeth (H1361) — who exalteth Himself to dwell; Psalm 113:5.
Saxon heah — high; Webster's root, later a courtesy title for princes and in Scripture a name for God's majesty.
usage: “By reason of his highness I could not endure” — transcendence as the brake on a powerful man.
“Them that rejoice in my highness” — the same attribute, met with gladness.
“High and lifted up” — and His train filled the temple.
